newsitem.title: USA: OLYMPICS-SALT LAKE CITY ROCKED BY OLYMPIC RESIGNATION.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-SALT LAKE CITY ROCKED BY OLYMPIC RESIGNATION.

text.p: Organisers of the 2002 Winter Olympic Games met behind closed doors Wednesday to find a replacement for the man who worked tirelessly to bring the Games to Utah but resigned in a wife-beating scandal.
Trustees of the Salt Lake City Organising Committee were also deciding whether Tom Welch should collect a $100,000-a-year pension after the Games.
Welch, 52, who gave up a $325,000-a-year job as SLOC president and chief executive officer, was likely to be kept on as a $10,000-a-month consultant, reports said.

One source told the Salt Lake City newspaper Deseret News there was some opposition to Welch getting the pension, since the plan was introduced specifically as an incentive to get officials to stay through 2002.

The trustees were also launching a nationwide search for a successor, with one name high on the list -- Dave Checketts, former president of the NBA's Utah Jazz and currently in charge of Madison Square Garden which houses basketball's New York Knicks and hockey's New York Rangers.
Welch, a former Mormon bishop known in Utah as "Mr Olympics," resigned Tuesday, eight days after being charged with domestic violence, which he denies.
According to police, he was charged with domestic violence battery, based on allegations he bruised and restrained his wife Alma during an argument over another woman.
His wife did not press charges but the authorities decided to go ahead with the case.
Welch, who was on an African safari with one of his six children when the charge was filed, returned to deny ever hitting his wife and acknowledged only "emotional ties" to an unnamed woman.
When he resigned, he said he was doing so to end the "feeding frenzy" surrounding the case in this staunchly conservative city that is home base for the Mormon Church.
"There are a lot of innocent people out here, including myself, who are getting devoured," Welch told reporters.

The Deseret News, which is owned by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints and reflects Mormon attitudes, said in an editorial the need to maintain the ultra-clean image was paramount in the deluge of news stories about Welch.
"Lest they tarnish the image Utah has tried to portray leading up to the Games, Welch needed to free SLOC from the burden he had become," it said.
Frank Joklik, Welch's deputy, said in a statement: "...our primary concern is to uphold the image of the Olympic movement and respect for its ideals."

Welch had worked since 1985 to bring the Winter Olympics to Utah. It lost out to Nagano, Japan, for the 1998 Games before landing the 2002 Games. He was named president and chief executive of the organising committee in 1995.
In Wednesday's editorial, the Deseret News said Welch's resignation was "for the best.
"The 2002 Winter Olympics are bigger than Tom Welch. They will put the entire state and its people on worldwide display."
The newspaper went on: "Welch was wise enough to understand how, even should he vindicate himself from the charges, his personal life had become too distracting."

However, it praised his efforts on behalf of Salt Lake City, saying: "Without his tireless efforts, both in the unsuccessful bid for the 1998 Games and the triumphant campaign for 2002, Utah would not be anxiously preparing to greet the world in five years."

In a statement Tuesday when he resigned, Welch said of his 12 years' work in bringing the Olympics to Utah: "While my family had many wonderful experiences along the way, we also exposed ourselves to long-term stresses which we neither recognised nor foresaw. One of the casualties was my marriage, which broke along the way. We were unable to repair it."
